docs.syntax: =MID(text,FIND("-",text)+1,4) finds the separator then slices after it; criteria take patterns
docs.explain: This screen is the two halves of text work in one place. The first half is a slice placed relative to a separator: FIND reports where the hyphen sits, one is added because the digits begin after it, and MID reads from there. Nothing in that formula is a typed number that depends on this particular table, which is what separates a formula from a transcription. The second half is the pattern in a criterion, where a star does the work that a whole list of region names would otherwise do. Both halves appear because real sheets mix them: an imported column arrives as one long string, and the reporting column beside it asks how many rows fit a pattern. The detail that trips people is that the two techniques answer different kinds of question. The slice returns a piece of text and has to be pinned to a position; the pattern returns a number and does not care where anything sits. Reading both off one table, as this screen does, makes the distinction concrete rather than theoretical.

screens.prompt: In D2, read the four digits that follow the hyphen in the code in A2.

hints.syntax: =MID(A2,FIND("-",A2)+1,4): FIND locates the hyphen, MID reads from just after it.
hints.func-mid: The digits are a slice of the code, so MID reads them.
hints.func-find: The hyphen moves between rows, so FIND works out where it sits.
hints.value: The hyphen is third, so the four digits start at four.
hints.error: If the code held no hyphen, FIND would fail with #VALUE!.

hints.syntax: =ROUND(AVERAGEIFS(C2:C5,B2:B5,"N*"),1): the averages first, the pattern last.

seo.title: Slice text with FIND and MID in Excel
seo.description: FIND says where the separator sits and MID reads from there. A wildcard criterion on the same screen shows why a pattern answers a different question.
